These violations contradict House Joint Resolution 192 ( HJR 192 ), Public Law 73-10 ( Emergency Banking Act ), the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), the U.S. Constitution, and various federal laws and regulations.

According to UCC 3-104 ( a ) and UCC 3-302 ( a ) ( 2 ), these instruments are valid as negotiable instruments, and I accepted these securities " for value, '' issuing a restrictive endorsement as outlined in UCC 3-206. Additionally, I affixed postage stamps ( lawful money ) to these securities under HJR 192 and UCC 1-201 ( b ) ( 24 ), reinforcing my payments.

Despite receiving these securities through registered and certified mail, [ Institution Name ] failed to discharge the debt, return the securities, or properly credit my account, in violation of UCC 3-603 ( b ). This provision mandates that any obligation is discharged to the extent of a payment made by a negotiable instrument unless that instrument is returned or dishonored. Their retention of the securities without action violates my rights as both a creditor and holder of the instruments.

Unlawful Closure of Accounts and Definition of " Accounts '' : It is important to clarify that the term account inherently means a place for deposits and withdrawals, not a static or limited financial agreement. As such, [ Institution Name ] unlawfully closed my accounts even after I had discharged the related debts through the lawful tender of securities. These accounts, by their nature, should be considered open-ended credit plans, which should not have a predetermined limit. Under my unlimited right to contract, as protected by the U.S. Constitution, I am entitled to maintain these accounts without arbitrary closure, particularly after meeting my financial obligations through lawful payments.

The attempt to impose artificial credit limits or close my accounts after the debt was discharged is unlawful. Showing limits on an open-ended credit plan, as [ Institution Name ] has done, is illegal and contrary to both the terms of open-ended credit and contract law principles. Their action constitutes a breach of UCC 3-311 concerning the resolution of debts through accord and satisfaction and violates my constitutional right to contract freely without interference.

Potential Fraud, Theft, and Securities Fraud : In addition to their mishandling of the securities and failure to honor my lawful payments, I am concerned that [ Institution Name ] may be engaging in fraudulent activities. Language fraud may also be present in the manner in which the terms of my accounts, securities, and payments have been communicated. [ Institution Name ] has used deceptive or unclear language that obscures the nature of my rights and obligations, particularly in regard to the use of lawful money and the nature of the securities provided. By misleading me about the status of the accounts and payments, they are potentially engaging in fraudulent misrepresentation under 18 U.S. Code 1341 ( Mail Fraud ) and 18 U.S. Code 1343 ( Wire Fraud ).

So I did just that. But on XX/XX/XXXX I received an email from Wells Fargo, telling me that my credit card application had been rejected. A letter would follow in the mail, explaining the reason ( s ) why.

I did indeed receive that letter, which stated : After a careful review, we are unable to approve your request for the following reasons : Income provided cant be verified.

Our decision was based in whole or in part on information in a credit report from the consumer reporting agency below. 

That would be XXXX. This letter was intended to explain why my application was rejected. But it just left me scratching my head. I sent the 1040 Forms that quoted both my taxable and tax-exempt income, so why the statement that my income cant be verified? As for XXXX, it deems my XXXX XXXX XXXX of XXXX, to be exceptional. Additionally, XXXX XXXX quotes my XXXX XXXX to be XXXX. XXXX quotes a XXXX XXXX of XXXX. So why am I being denied credit at this particular time, from this particular bank? Im registered at XXXX, and under the menu item How do lenders see me?, XXXX writes, Currently lenders may see you as extremely reliable. Heres why : Exceptional Credit Rating.

Low Credit Usage.

Excellent Payment History.

Exceptional Credit History Length.

Low Estimated Debt-to-income. '' So what gives? I never had a problem acquiring a new line of credit, until now. And I dont have a problem with the rejection per se, as much as I do the inadequacy of the explanation.

So I called the Wells Fargo Credit Departments customer service line, provided to field questions. I stated all of the above to the rep, and speculated as to whether my recent history as a victim of identity theft may have influenced the banks decision. Well yes, she saidbecause I had placed an Alert on my account at the 3 credit rating agencies, warning any potential lender to verify my identity before extending a new line of credit. It would have been helpful, made sense to me, if Wells Fargo had stated that in their explanatory letter. But no matter ; the rep said it hadnt been a hard rejection. And this call would serve as proof of my identity. She would refile my application and didnt anticipate any problems. 

But on XX/XX/XXXX I received a 2nd rejection via email, with the same promise of a letter to follow, by way of explanation. And I did indeed receive that letter. Our decision was based in whole or in part on information in a credit report from the consumer reporting agency below.

Thank you Wells Fargo. That was helpful.

I mentioned that Id only sent the 1st page of my XXXX & XXXX Form 1040, as they contained the relevant info requested vis-a-vis my income, and I assumed that would suffice. What? Everyone knows by now, its the wild west out there. Were taught to be careful with the information we share, and for good reason. And does Wells Fargo not owe me a true explanation, one that makes sense, for why my application was denied?

I believe on this phone call, the customer service agent was able to provide me with the reasoning for my account closure and was surprised that previous customer service representatives were unable to provide me with the information. The reasons given stated that my income could not be verified. I informed the representative that I was told to provide account statements from my primary account only, which accounted for most but not all of my income. Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1601 - Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) The Truth in Lending Act requires creditors to provide clear, accurate, and meaningful disclosures to consumers regarding credit decisions. 4. Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1691 - Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( ECOA ) The Equal Credit Opportunity Act requires creditors to provide specific, actionable reasons for denying credit. The adverse action notice I received uses vague and general language that does not meet the ECOAs requirements for clarity. Information about applicable regulations currently in effect can be found at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 's website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
NOTICE TO FURNISHERS OF INFORMATION : OBLIGATIONS OF FURNISHERS UNDER THE FCRA The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681-1681y, imposes responsibilities on all persons who furnish information to consumer reporting agencies ( CRAs ). These responsibilities are found in Section 623 of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2. State law may impose additional requirements on furnishers. All furnishers of information to CRAs should become familiar with the applicable laws and may want to consult with their counsel to ensure that they are in compliance. 
The text of the FCRA is set forth in full at the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection 's website at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. A list of the sections of the FCRA cross-referenced to the U.S. Code is at the end of this document. 
Section 623 imposes the following duties : Accuracy Guidelines The banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will promulgate guidelines and regulations dealing with the accuracy of information provided to CRAs by furnishers. The regulations and guidelines issued by the CFPB will be available at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore when they are issued. Section 623 ( e ). 
General Prohibition on Reporting Inaccurate Information The FCRA prohibits information furnishers from providing information to a CRA that they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. However, the furnisher is not subject to this general prohibition if it clearly and conspicuously specifies an address to which consumers may write to notify the furnisher that certain information is inaccurate. Sections 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( a ) ( 1 ) ( C ). 
Duty to Correct and Update Information If at any time a person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs determines that the information provided is not complete or accurate, the furnisher must promptly provide complete and accurate information to the CRA. In addition, the furnisher must notify all CRAs that received the information of any corrections, and must thereafter report only the complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). 
Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer If a consumer notifies a furnisher, at an address specified by the furnisher for such notices, that specific information is inaccurate, and the information is, in fact, inaccurate, the furnisher must thereafter report the correct information to CRAs. 
Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ). 
If a consumer notifies a furnisher that the consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of any information reported by the furnisher, the furnisher may not subsequently report that information to a CRA without providing notice of the dispute. 
Section 623 ( a ) ( 3 ). 
The federal banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will issue regulations that will identify when an information furnisher must investigate a dispute made directly to the furnisher by a consumer. Once these regulations are issued, furnishers must comply with them and complete an investigation within 30 days ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information ) unless the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant or comes from a credit repair organization. The CFPB regulations will be available at consumerfinance.gov. Section 623 ( a ) ( 8 ). 
Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer Reporting Agency If a CRA notifies a furnisher that a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of information provided by the furnisher, the furnisher has a duty to follow certain procedures. The furnisher must : Conduct an investigation and review all relevant information provided by the CRA, including information given to the CRA by the consumer. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

Report the results to the CRA that referred the dispute, and, if the investigation establishes that the information was, in fact, incomplete or inaccurate, report the results to all CRAs to which the furnisher provided the information that compile and maintain files on a nationwide basis. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( C ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ).

Complete the above steps within 30 days from the date the CRA receives the dispute ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information to the CRA ). Section 623 ( b ) ( 2 ).

Promptly modify or delete the information, or block its reporting. Section 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( E ).

Duty to Report Voluntary Closing of Credit Accounts If a consumer voluntarily closes a credit account, any person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs must report this fact when it provides information to CRAs for the time period in which the account was closed. Section 623 ( a ) ( 4 ).

Duty to Report Dates of Delinquencies If a furnisher reports information concerning a delinquent account placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subject to any similar action, the furnisher must, within 90 days after reporting the information, provide the CRA with the month and the year of the commencement of the delinquency that immediately preceded the action, so that the agency will know how long to keep the information in the consumer 's file. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Any person, such as a debt collector, that has acquired or is responsible for collecting delinquent accounts and that reports information to CRAs may comply with the requirements of Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( until there is a consumer dispute ) by reporting the same delinquency date previously reported by the creditor. If the creditor did not report this date, they may comply with the FCRA by establishing reasonable procedures to obtain and report delinquency dates, or, if a delinquency date can not be reasonably obtained, by following reasonable procedures to ensure that the date reported precedes the date when the account was placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Duties of Financial Institutions When Reporting Negative Information Financial institutions that furnish information to nationwide consumer reporting agencies, as defined in Section 603 ( p ), must notify consumers in writing if they may furnish or have furnished negative information to a CRA. Section 623 ( a ) ( 7 ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has prescribed model disclosures, 12 CFR Part 1022, App. B. 
Duties When Furnishing Medical Information A furnisher whose primary business is providing medical services, products, or devices ( and such furnisher 's agents or assignees ) is a medical information furnisher for the purposes of the FCRA and must notify all CRAs to which it reports of this fact. Section 623 ( a ) ( 9 ). This notice will enable CRAs to comply with their duties under Section 604 ( g ) when reporting medical information. 
Duties when ID Theft Occurs All furnishers must have in place reasonable procedures to respond to notifications from CRAs that information furnished is the result of identity theft, and to prevent refurnishing the information in the future. A furnisher may not furnish information that a consumer has identified as resulting from identity theft unless the furnisher subsequently knows or is informed by the consumer that the information is correct. Section 623 ( a ) ( 6 ). If a furnisher learns that it has furnished inaccurate information due to identity theft, it must notify each consumer reporting agency of the correct information and must thereafter report only complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). When any furnisher of information is notified pursuant to the procedures set forth in Section 605B that a debt has resulted from identity theft, the furnisher may not sell, transfer, or place for collection the debt except in certain limited circumstances. Section 615 ( f ). 
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore, has more information about the FCRA.

Dear CFPB, I am writing to file a formal complaint against Navy Federal Credit Union for the unlawful closure of my credit card account, which took place on XX/XX/year>. The circumstances surrounding the closure of this account raise serious concerns regarding potential violations of several federal consumer protection laws, and I am seeking the CFPB 's immediate intervention in this matter. 

Background of the Situation : On XX/XX/year>, I was contacted by a representative from Navy Federal 's in-house collections team regarding my credit card account, which was two months past due. During this conversation, I was informed of financial hardship options designed to keep my account active. The representative assured me that my interest rate would be reduced to 3 % for a period of 12 months and that Navy Federal would be evaluating my eligibility for an additional financial program. At no point was I informed that my account was under consideration for closure. 

However, on XX/XX/year>, just three days later and prior to receiving any further communication about my eligibility for the financial program, Navy Federal closed my account without notice. This abrupt action was unexpected and contrary to the information provided during the XX/XX/XXXX call, during which I was led to believe that my account was still active and being reviewed for assistance. 

Violations of Consumer Protection Laws : Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Violation : Navy Federals failure to provide complete and accurate information about the status of my account during our XX/XX/XXXX conversation violates the FCRA. The closure of the account without proper notification has likely caused adverse effects on my credit report, and I was not given an opportunity to address or prevent this negative outcome. 
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ) Violation : The communication from Navy Federal was misleading, as I was led to believe that my account was being offered hardship options and would remain active. The sudden closure of the account, without disclosing that it was being targeted for shutdown, constitutes deceptive and unfair collection practices, in violation of the FDCPA. 

Breach of Good Faith and Fair Dealing : By failing to inform me of the true status of my account and then closing it without warning, Navy Federal breached the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. I was denied the opportunity to make informed decisions regarding my account and was misled into believing that it was being maintained in good standing. 

Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) Violation : Navy Federals actions may also constitute a violation of TILA, which requires creditors to provide clear and accurate disclosures about the terms and conditions of credit. The failure to inform me of the impending closure of my account while discussing potential hardship programs falls short of these requirements.

Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, I am writing to formally file a complaint against Comenity Bank regarding what I believe to be deceptive billing practices that have severely impacted my financial situation. 

In or around XX/XX/year>, I made a purchase using a promotion offered by Comenity Bank that provided 24 months of interest-free financing. To ensure I remained compliant with the terms of this promotion, I promptly set up an auto payment for the minimum amount due on my account. My understanding was that this would cover my obligations related to the promotional offer. 

Approximately one year later, I made an additional purchase using the same promotion. I assumed that my auto payment settings would continue to automatically cover the minimum amount due, as I had previously established. However, to my shock, I was recently notified by XXXX XXXX that one of my accounts had exceeded the credit limit. Concerned, I contacted Comenity Bank to investigate the issue. 

During my conversation with Comenity Bank, I was informed that their billing system does not automatically adjust auto payments when new purchases are made. This means that even though my obligations were increasing, my auto payments remained tied to the original amount I set up, which led to an unintentional failure to cover my balances over time. I was further told that the auto payment option I selected is based on a specific amount, despite the label indicating it was for the minimum payment due. This information is alarming and highlights a lack of transparency in their billing practices. 

If Comenity Bank 's claims are accurate, I believe I should have been charged a late fee when I failed to meet the adjusted minimum payment amount a year ago. Such a charge would have alerted me to the fact that my financial obligations were increasing. However, I never received any communication regarding changes to my payment amounts or missed payments, despite making payments of {$5400.00} over the past 24 months. 

Overall, I find it deeply concerning that Comenity Bank has not taken responsibility for this situation. I have never missed a payment, and I have actively stayed engaged in maintaining my account in good standing. The lack of notification about the increase in my minimum payment and the inability of their auto payment system to reflect my new obligations feels intentionally deceptive. 

In light of these issues, I respectfully urge the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to investigate these practices at Comenity Bank. It is imperative that financial institutions adhere to fair and transparent billing practices to protect consumers from potential exploitation. If such practices are indeed part of a larger scheme to defraud customers, action must be taken to hold Comenity Bank accountable. 

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your response and any guidance you can provide on how to proceed.

NOTICE TO FURNISHERS OF INFORMATION : OBLIGATIONS OF FURNISHERS UNDER THE FCRA The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681-1681y, imposes responsibilities on all persons who furnish information to consumer reporting agencies ( CRAs ). These responsibilities are found in Section 623 of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2. State law may impose additional requirements on furnishers. All furnishers of information to CRAs should become familiar with the applicable laws and may want to consult with their counsel to ensure that they are in compliance. 
The text of the FCRA is set forth in full at the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection 's website at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. A list of the sections of the FCRA cross-referenced to the U.S. Code is at the end of this document. 
Section 623 imposes the following duties : Accuracy Guidelines The banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will promulgate guidelines and regulations dealing with the accuracy of information provided to CRAs by furnishers. The regulations and guidelines issued by the CFPB will be available at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore when they are issued. Section 623 ( e ). 
General Prohibition on Reporting Inaccurate Information The FCRA prohibits information furnishers from providing information to a CRA that they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. However, the furnisher is not subject to this general prohibition if it clearly and conspicuously specifies an address to which consumers may write to notify the furnisher that certain information is inaccurate. Sections 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( a ) ( 1 ) ( C ). 
Duty to Correct and Update Information If at any time a person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs determines that the information provided is not complete or accurate, the furnisher must promptly provide complete and accurate information to the CRA. In addition, the furnisher must notify all CRAs that received the information of any corrections, and must thereafter report only the complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). 
Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer If a consumer notifies a furnisher, at an address specified by the furnisher for such notices, that specific information is inaccurate, and the information is, in fact, inaccurate, the furnisher must thereafter report the correct information to CRAs. 
Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

If a consumer notifies a furnisher that the consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of any information reported by the furnisher, the furnisher may not subsequently report that information to a CRA without providing notice of the dispute. 
Section 623 ( a ) ( 3 ).

The federal banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will issue regulations that will identify when an information furnisher must investigate a dispute made directly to the furnisher by a consumer. Once these regulations are issued, furnishers must comply with them and complete an investigation within 30 days ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information ) unless the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant or comes from a credit repair organization. The CFPB regulations will be available at consumerfinance.gov. Section 623 ( a ) ( 8 ). 
Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer Reporting Agency If a CRA notifies a furnisher that a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of information provided by the furnisher, the furnisher has a duty to follow certain procedures. The furnisher must : Conduct an investigation and review all relevant information provided by the CRA, including information given to the CRA by the consumer. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( B ). 

Report the results to the CRA that referred the dispute, and, if the investigation establishes that the information was, in fact, incomplete or inaccurate, report the results to all CRAs to which the furnisher provided the information that compile and maintain files on a nationwide basis. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( C ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ). 

Complete the above steps within 30 days from the date the CRA receives the dispute ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information to the CRA ). Section 623 ( b ) ( 2 ).

Promptly modify or delete the information, or block its reporting. Section 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( E ).

Duty to Report Voluntary Closing of Credit Accounts If a consumer voluntarily closes a credit account, any person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs must report this fact when it provides information to CRAs for the time period in which the account was closed. Section 623 ( a ) ( 4 ). 
Duty to Report Dates of Delinquencies If a furnisher reports information concerning a delinquent account placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subject to any similar action, the furnisher must, within 90 days after reporting the information, provide the CRA with the month and the year of the commencement of the delinquency that immediately preceded the action, so that the agency will know how long to keep the information in the consumer 's file. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ). 
Any person, such as a debt collector, that has acquired or is responsible for collecting delinquent accounts and that reports information to CRAs may comply with the requirements of Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( until there is a consumer dispute ) by reporting the same delinquency date previously reported by the creditor. If the creditor did not report this date, they may comply with the FCRA by establishing reasonable procedures to obtain and report delinquency dates, or, if a delinquency date can not be reasonably obtained, by following reasonable procedures to ensure that the date reported precedes the date when the account was placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ). 
Duties of Financial Institutions When Reporting Negative Information Financial institutions that furnish information to nationwide consumer reporting agencies, as defined in Section 603 ( p ), must notify consumers in writing if they may furnish or have furnished negative information to a CRA. Section 623 ( a ) ( 7 ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has prescribed model disclosures, 12 CFR Part 1022, App. B. 
Duties When Furnishing Medical Information A furnisher whose primary business is providing medical services, products, or devices ( and such furnisher 's agents or assignees ) is a medical information furnisher for the purposes of the FCRA and must notify all CRAs to which it reports of this fact. Section 623 ( a ) ( 9 ). This notice will enable CRAs to comply with their duties under Section 604 ( g ) when reporting medical information. 
Duties when ID Theft Occurs All furnishers must have in place reasonable procedures to respond to notifications from CRAs that information furnished is the result of identity theft, and to prevent refurnishing the information in the future. A furnisher may not furnish information that a consumer has identified as resulting from identity theft unless the furnisher subsequently knows or is informed by the consumer that the information is correct. Section 623 ( a ) ( 6 ). If a furnisher learns that it has furnished inaccurate information due to identity theft, it must notify each consumer reporting agency of the correct information and must thereafter report only complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). When any furnisher of information is notified pursuant to the procedures set forth in Section 605B that a debt has resulted from identity theft, the furnisher may not sell, transfer, or place for collection the debt except in certain limited circumstances. Section 615 ( f ).

The letter informed me that this decision was based on my non-response to a request for additional information. I find this concerning, as it implies that the investigation may not have been thorough and that the burden of proof was improperly shifted onto me as the consumer. Consumer complaint narrative:
You can incorporate the timing details and mention of the replacement card into the existing narrative like this : On Friday, XX/XX/2024, I received notice that my account was closed due to " one or more occurrences of late or returned payments in the last six months. '' However, after speaking with a representative XXXX XXXX, Reference # XXXX ), I was told there were no late payments but three returned payments : on XXXX and XXXX for {$600.00} each, and on XXXX for {$6900.00}. 

The returned payments were caused by a misleading " Apply '' button located next to the " Other Amount '' input field on the payment page. The button, now removed, led to confusion about its purpose, causing the unintended submission of payments. When I realized the error, I was told the initial payments could not be canceled, putting me in a dire financial position. This also triggered the additional returned payments. The screenshots attached show the " Apply '' button before its removal and the updated interface. 

When the returned payments occurred, I contacted customer service and was assured they would be forgiven, with no penalties applied. Relying on this assurance, I continued to use the card and increased my balance, assuming the card would remain available through the holiday season. Now, nearly four months after the returned payments, I find myself facing an unforeseen account closure just days after receiving and activating a replacement card that I can no longer use due to this abrupt action.

This " Apply '' button appears to have been intentionally designed to confuse users, leading to accidental payments. Its placement near the input field, lack of clear communication, and absence of confirmation steps encouraged accidental clicks. Once payments were submitted, they couldnt be canceled, trapping users financially. The companys representatives provided misleading assurances about the impact of the returned payments, further exacerbating harm. 

This deceptive design likely benefited the company through fees from returned payments, late charges, and increased interest on balances. It also justified account closures, allowing the company to recover debt and void user rewards. Changes to the website obscured the misleading design and hindered dispute resolution. These actions suggest a deliberate strategy to exploit users for financial gain. I urge the CFPB to investigate this practice, provide restitution, and ensure similar actions are prevented in the future. 

In addition, when I was transferred to an Adverse Action Department representative ( XXXX ) regarding the closure of my account, I was told that the Adverse Action Department does not record or provide reference numbers for call occurrences. This practice, if true, appears to benefit the company by limiting accountability, as customers can not easily prove what was said during a call or verify assurances provided by representatives. It also hinders dispute resolution, making it more challenging for customers to follow up or contest adverse decisions without a record of the interaction. Furthermore, the lack of reference numbers reduces the companys exposure to legal or regulatory scrutiny, as there is less documented evidence available for review in case of complaints or investigations. This opacity also obscures the companys internal practices, making it difficult to confirm whether policies are being followed consistently. Additionally, the absence of reference numbers may discourage customers from pursuing complaints, as it creates frustration and a perception that their concerns will not be addressed effectively. By minimizing the documentation of such interactions, the company reduces its likelihood of having to offer restitution or reverse adverse decisions, further benefiting from this lack of transparency.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am writing as a concerned customer of Truist Bank, specifically in relation to my business account with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which was offered a 0 % interest promotion for 12 months. Despite my efforts to ensure full compliance with all the promotional terms, Truist Bank recently revoked this offer, and I am compelled to address this as both a loyal customer and a consumer advocating for fair treatment under the law. 



My intent has been to comply with the requirements fully, ensuring all payments are made on time. To that end, I set up auto-pay on my account, confirmed this with a Truist representative, and requested physical statements as an additional safeguard to prevent any oversight. I logged into my account regularly, verifying each month that no payment was due and confirming that the auto-pay system was functioning as it should. Unfortunately, I was unable to hear him clearly due to technical issues on his end, which I reported multiple times. After several attempts on different devices and with no escalation to a supervisor despite my requests, this unresolved matter has left me frustrated and without a solution. 



As a consumer, I am protected under the Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act ( CARD Act ) of 2009, which prohibits credit card issuers from arbitrarily revoking promotional interest rates if the customer has complied with the terms. Section 1026.55 ( c ) ( 2 ) of Regulation Z of the Truth in Lending Act further states that issuers must provide clear disclosures on conditions and can not impose unexpected fees or rate increases, especially in cases where a consumer has demonstrated good faith efforts to meet the promotions requirements. In this instance, Truist Banks cancellation of my 0 % interest rate promotion contradicts both the spirit and the letter of these consumer protections. 



I ask that you review this matter with urgency, taking into account my proactive steps to comply with the promotional guidelines, as well as the lack of proper support and communication from Truist representatives when I sought resolution. I respectfully request that my 0 % promotional rate be reinstated and that any late fees or penalties resulting from this situation be reversed. 



Please consider this as an opportunity for Truist to reinforce its commitment to customer service, transparency, and regulatory compliance. I trust that, in light of the circumstances, you will take appropriate corrective action.

This provision mandates that any obligation is discharged to the extent of a payment made by a negotiable instrument unless that instrument is returned or dishonored. As such, CITIBANK Credit/Banking Institution unlawfully closed my accounts even after I had discharged the related debts through the lawful tender of securities. These accounts, by their nature, should be considered open-ended credit plans, which should not have a predetermined limit. Under my unlimited right to contract, as protected by the U.S. Constitution, I am entitled to maintain these accounts without arbitrary closure, particularly after meeting my financial obligations through lawful payments.

CITIBANK Credit/Banking Institution has used deceptive or unclear language that obscures the nature of my rights and obligations, particularly in regard to the use of lawful money and the nature of the securities provided. By misleading me about the status of the accounts and payments, they are potentially engaging in fraudulent misrepresentation under 18 U.S. Code 1341 ( Mail Fraud ) and 18 U.S. Code 1343 ( Wire Fraud ).

[ Institution Name ], by refusing to honor my position as the holder of these instruments, has violated my holder-in-due-course rights. They retained the securities without processing them, have continued to unlawfully demand further payments, and have denied my rightful claim to the value of these instruments, in violation of UCC 3-305 ( concerning defenses and claims to an instrument ).

The improper handling of these private instruments suggests potential violations of 15 U.S. Code Chapter 41- Consumer Credit Protection. 
Failure to Discharge Debt Under the Emergency Banking Act and Gold Clause : According to Public Law 73-10 ( Emergency Banking Act ) and HJR 192, all debts must be discharged upon the tender of lawful money. My payment, which consisted of securities and lawful money ( postage stamps ), fully satisfied the obligation. UCC 1-201 ( b ) ( 24 ) : Defines lawful money, including postage stamps affixed to negotiable instruments. 
12 U.S. Code 411 : Governs the issuance and receipt of lawful money and its proper application in discharging debts.

Deceptive Acts or Practices A three-part test is used to determine whether a representation, omission, or practice is deceptive. This test was first laid out in the FTC Policy Statement on Deceptive Acts and Practices.8 First, the representation, omission, or practice must mislead or be likely to mislead the consumer. Second, the consumers interpretation of the representation, omission, or practice must be reasonable under the circumstances. Third, the misleading representation, omission, or practice must be material. 9 As a general matter, the standards for establishing deception less burdensome than the standards for establishing unfairness because, under deception, there is no requirement of substantial injury or the likelihood of substantial injury, or the other elements of unfairness related to consumer injury. The following discusses all three of the elements necessary to establish deception.10 There must be a representation, omission, or practice that misleads or is likely to mislead the consumer. An act or practice may be found to be deceptive if there is a representation, omission, or practice that misleads or is likely to mislead a consumer. Deception is not limited to situations in which a consumer has already been misled. Instead, an act or practice may be found to be deceptive if it is likely to mislead consumers. A representation may be in the form of express or implied claims or promises and may be written or oral. Omission of information may be deceptive if disclosure of the omitted information is necessary to prevent a consumer from being misled. An individual statement, representation, or omission is not evaluated in isolation to determine if it is misleading, but rather in the context of the entire advertisement, transaction, or course of dealing. Acts or practices that have the potentialto be deceptive include : making misleading cost or price claims ; using bait-and-switch techniques; offering to provide a product or service that is not in fact available ; omitting material limitations or conditions from an offer ; selling a product unfit for the purposes for which it is sold ; and failing to provide promised services. The act or practice must be considered from the perspective of the reasonable consumer. In determining whether an act or practice is misleading, the consumers interpretation of or reaction to the representation, omission, or practice must be reasonable under the circumstances. In other words, whether an act or practice is deceptive depends on how a reasonable member of the target audience would interpret the marketing material. When representations or marketing practices are targeted to a specific audience, such as the elderly or the financially unsophisticated, the communication is reviewed from the point of view of a reasonable member of that group. ____________________ 10 Clear and Conspicuous Disclosures When evaluating the three-part test for deception, the four Ps should be considered : prominence, presentation, placement, and proximity. First, is the statement prominent enough for the consumer to notice? Second, is the information presented in an easy to understand format that does not contradict other information in the package and at a time when the consumers attention is not distracted elsewhere? Third, is the placement of the information in a location where consumers can be expected to look or hear? Finally, is the information in close proximity to the claim it qualifies? More information is available at : XXXX XXXX XXXX If a representation conveys two or more meanings to reasonable consumers and one meaning is misleading, the representation may be deceptive. Moreover, a consumers interpretation or reaction may indicate that an act or practice is deceptive under the circumstances, even if the consumers interpretation is not shared by a majority of the consumers in the relevant class, so long as a significant minority of such consumers is misled. Written disclosures may be insufficient to correct a misleading statement or representation, particularly where the consumer is directed away from qualifying limitations in the text or is counseled that reading the disclosures is unnecessary. Likewise, oral disclosures or fine print are generally insufficient to cure a misleading headline or prominent written representation. Finally, a deceptive act or practice can not be cured by subsequent truthful disclosures. The representation, omission, or practice must be material. A representation, omission, or practice is material if it is likely to affect a consumers decision to purchase or use a product or service. In general, information about costs, benefits, or restrictions on the use or availability of a product or service is material. When express claims are made with respect to a financial product or service, the claims will be presumed to be material. While intent to deceive is not a required element of proving that an act or practice is deceptive, the materiality of an implied claim will be presumed if it can be shown that the institution intended that the consumer draw certain conclusions based upon the claim. Claims made with knowledge that they are false will also be presumed to be material. Background : On XX/XX/year>, I applied for the American Express Platinum Card, providing all required personal and financial information. American Express denied my application based on information from my consumer report, despite knowing that the information was false and unverifiable. Following this denial, I submitted XXXX notarized affidavits on XX/XX/year>, and XX/XX/year>, asserting that the consumer report data used was inaccurate and demanding lawful justification, verification of the method used, and compliance with federal consumer protection laws. Along with these affidavits, I submitted an invoice for {$49000.00} in damages. Despite this, American Express has not reversed the denial or taken corrective action, effectively agreeing to the statements in my affidavits under UCC 1-205 by failing to respond. 

Violations Cited : Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1691 ) American Expresss denial of my credit application appears to lack a lawful and objective basis, suggesting discriminatory practices. This violates ECOA, which mandates equal and fair treatment in credit decisions. 

Truth in Lending Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq. ) TILA requires clear disclosure of credit terms and finance charges. American Express did not provide essential disclosures, including my right of rescission, and failed to clarify how my Social Security number was used in the decision, contravening TILAs transparency requirements. 

Fair Credit Reporting Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. ) American Express based its decision on my consumer report data without my consent and did not provide the legally required verification method. Despite knowing the consumer report information was false, they used it to deny my application, violating my rights under FCRA. 

Failure to Respond to Notarized Affidavits and Invoice Under UCC 1-205, unrebutted affidavits stand as true by law. By not responding to my affidavits and the {$49000.00} invoice within the required period, American Express tacitly agreed to the statements and charges within, further demonstrating non-compliance with consumer protections. 

Use of Unauthorized Credit Data and Potential Harassment American Express sent duplicate denial notices, which may constitute intimidation under 15 U.S.C. 1692. This unnecessary repetition, without a lawful basis for denial, violates protections against consumer harassment. 

Relief Sought : Approval of the American Express Platinum Card Based on my documented affidavits and statutory rights, I request immediate reconsideration and approval of my credit application. 

Compensation for Damages I seek the invoiced amount of {$49000.00} in damages due to American Expresss non-compliance with federal statutes and associated legal costs, in addition to accountability for finance charges disclosed under TILA but not honored. 

Full Disclosure of Credit Denial Reasons and Verification Method American Express must provide a clear explanation of the factors and verification methods used in their decision and correct their reliance on false data in my consumer report. 

Conclusion and Next Steps : I request that the CFPB investigate American Express for non-compliance with ECOA, TILA, FCRA, and related consumer protection laws, as documented in my affidavits and invoiced demand. If American Express does not take corrective action within 10 business days, I will pursue further legal remedies, including arbitration and statutory claims under federal law. 

Attachment : Invoice for Damages ( {$49000.00} ) Thank you for your assistance in addressing these violations of consumer rights. 

Respectfully Submitted, XXXX XXXX XXXX

This is a near XXXX XXXX XXXX credit card with a {$8000.00} limit and a XXXX XXXX payment history. I was missed one or two payment due dates and they closed the card without any hesitation. Consumer complaint narrative:
Subject : Formal Complaint Against Bank of America for Deceptive Practices Regarding 0 % APR Promotional Expiration Leading to Unjust Finance Charges To the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) : I am submitting this formal complaint against Bank of America ( BOA ) for engaging in deceptive and potentially unlawful practices regarding the disclosure of the expiration date of a 0 % APR promotional offer on my credit card accounts ( Account # 1 : XXXX and Account # 2 : XXXX ). BOA 's failure to transparently communicate the termination of this promotional period has resulted in unexpected and unjust finance charges, despite my adherence to responsible credit management practices. 


Background : In XX/XX/year>, BOA extended a 0 % APR promotional offer on my credit card accounts ( Account # 1 and Account # 2 ). Throughout the promotional period, BOA failed to disclose the specific expiration date of this offer in any monthly statements or communications. They never show that information hoping that the customer will forget to pay in full on time. I am attaching snapshots from my most recent statements dated XX/XX/year>, as proof. Consequently, on XX/XX/year>, I was assessed the following finance charges : Account # 1, ending in XXXX : {$35.00} finance charge Account # 2, ending in XXXX : {$19.00} finance charge These charges were applied despite my consistent payments during the promotion period and full payments on both accounts, under the reasonable assumption that the 0 % APR promotion was still in effect. 

Legal Concerns : BOA 's omission of the promotional expiration date constitutes a violation of the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), which mandates clear and conspicuous disclosure of credit terms to consumers. Specifically, Regulation Z of TILA requires creditors to provide accurate information about finance charges and terms of credit. BOA 's failure to disclose the expiration date of the 0 % APR promotion impedes consumers ' ability to make informed financial decisions, thereby violating these provisions. 

Furthermore, this practice may contravene the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act 's prohibition against unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ). By withholding critical information, BOA has engaged in deceptive practices that mislead consumers regarding the true cost of credit.

Precedent and Consumer Impact : This issue is not isolated. Similar complaints have been documented, indicating a pattern of BOA 's nondisclosure of promotional term expirations, leading to unexpected finance charges for consumers. Such practices not only erode consumer trust but also suggest a systemic issue within BOA 's disclosure policies that warrants regulatory scrutiny. 

Requested Action : I urge the CFPB to : Investigate BOA 's disclosure practices concerning promotional APR offers to determine compliance with TILA and UDAAP provisions. 

Mandate that BOA provide clear and conspicuous disclosure of promotional terms, including expiration dates, in all relevant communications and monthly statements. 

Require BOA to refund all finance charges improperly levied due to nondisclosure of promotional expirations and to compensate affected consumers for any resulting financial harm. 

Implement industry-wide guidelines ensuring that all financial institutions adhere to transparent disclosure practices for promotional credit offers. 

By addressing these concerns, the CFPB will uphold its mandate to protect consumers from deceptive financial practices and ensure fair treatment in the credit market. 

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I trust that the CFPB will take appropriate action to rectify these deceptive practices and prevent further consumer harm.

Dear Sir or Madam : I am a victim of identity theft. I recently learned that my personal information was used to open an account at your company. I did not open or authorize this account, and I therefore request that it be closed immediately. I also request that your company absolve me of all charges on the account, and that you take all appropriate steps to remove information about this account from my credit files. 

Enclosed is a copy of my Identity Theft Report supporting my position, and a copy of my credit report showing the fraudulent items related to your company that are the result of identity theft. Also enclosed is a copy of the CFPBs Notice to Furnishers of Information, which details your responsibilities as an information furnisher to credit reporting agencies ( CRAs ). As a furnisher, upon receipt of a consumers written request that encloses an Identity Theft Report, you are required to cease furnishing the information resulting from identity theft to any CRA. 
The Notice also specifies your responsibilities when you receive notice from a CRA, under section 605B of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, that information you provided to the CRA may be the result of identity theft. Those responsibilities include ceasing to provide the inaccurate information to any CRAs and ensuring that you do not attempt to sell or transfer the fraudulent debts to another party for collection. 
Please investigate this matter, close the account and absolve me of all charges, take the steps required under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and send me a letter explaining your findings and actions. 
Sincerely, [ XXXX XXXX XXXX ] All furnishers of consumer reports must comply with all applicable regulations, including regulations promulgated after this notice was first prescribed in 2004. Information about applicable regulations currently in effect can be found at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 's website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. 
NOTICE TO FURNISHERS OF INFORMATION : OBLIGATIONS OF FURNISHERS UNDER THE FCRA The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681-1681y, imposes responsibilities on all persons who furnish information to consumer reporting agencies ( CRAs ). These responsibilities are found in Section 623 of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2. State law may impose additional requirements on furnishers. All furnishers of information to CRAs should become familiar with the applicable laws and may want to consult with their counsel to ensure that they are in compliance.

The text of the FCRA is set forth in full at the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection 's website at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore. A list of the sections of the FCRA cross-referenced to the U.S. Code is at the end of this document.

Section 623 imposes the following duties : Accuracy Guidelines The banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will promulgate guidelines and regulations dealing with the accuracy of information provided to CRAs by furnishers. The regulations and guidelines issued by the CFPB will be available at consumerfinance.gov/learnmore when they are issued. Section 623 ( e ).

General Prohibition on Reporting Inaccurate Information The FCRA prohibits information furnishers from providing information to a CRA that they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. However, the furnisher is not subject to this general prohibition if it clearly and conspicuously specifies an address to which consumers may write to notify the furnisher that certain information is inaccurate. Sections 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( a ) ( 1 ) ( C ).

Duty to Correct and Update Information If at any time a person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs determines that the information provided is not complete or accurate, the furnisher must promptly provide complete and accurate information to the CRA. In addition, the furnisher must notify all CRAs that received the information of any corrections, and must thereafter report only the complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ).

Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer If a consumer notifies a furnisher, at an address specified by the furnisher for such notices, that specific information is inaccurate, and the information is, in fact, inaccurate, the furnisher must thereafter report the correct information to CRAs.

Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

If a consumer notifies a furnisher that the consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of any information reported by the furnisher, the furnisher may not subsequently report that information to a CRA without providing notice of the dispute.

Section 623 ( a ) ( 3 ).

The federal banking and credit union regulators and the CFPB will issue regulations that will identify when an information furnisher must investigate a dispute made directly to the furnisher by a consumer. Once these regulations are issued, furnishers must comply with them and complete an investigation within 30 days ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information ) unless the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant or comes from a credit repair organization. The CFPB regulations will be available at consumerfinance.gov. Section 623 ( a ) ( 8 ).

Duties After Notice of Dispute from Consumer Reporting Agency If a CRA notifies a furnisher that a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of information provided by the furnisher, the furnisher has a duty to follow certain procedures. The furnisher must : Conduct an investigation and review all relevant information provided by the CRA, including information given to the CRA by the consumer. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( B ).

Report the results to the CRA that referred the dispute, and, if the investigation establishes that the information was, in fact, incomplete or inaccurate, report the results to all CRAs to which the furnisher provided the information that compile and maintain files on a nationwide basis. Sections 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( C ) and ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ).

Complete the above steps within 30 days from the date the CRA receives the dispute ( or 45 days, if the consumer later provides relevant additional information to the CRA ). Section 623 ( b ) ( 2 ).

Promptly modify or delete the information, or block its reporting. Section 623 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( E ).

Duty to Report Voluntary Closing of Credit Accounts If a consumer voluntarily closes a credit account, any person who regularly and in the ordinary course of business furnishes information to one or more CRAs must report this fact when it provides information to CRAs for the time period in which the account was closed. Section 623 ( a ) ( 4 ).

Duty to Report Dates of Delinquencies If a furnisher reports information concerning a delinquent account placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subject to any similar action, the furnisher must, within 90 days after reporting the information, provide the CRA with the month and the year of the commencement of the delinquency that immediately preceded the action, so that the agency will know how long to keep the information in the consumer 's file. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Any person, such as a debt collector, that has acquired or is responsible for collecting delinquent accounts and that reports information to CRAs may comply with the requirements of Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( until there is a consumer dispute ) by reporting the same delinquency date previously reported by the creditor. If the creditor did not report this date, they may comply with the FCRA by establishing reasonable procedures to obtain and report delinquency dates, or, if a delinquency date can not be reasonably obtained, by following reasonable procedures to ensure that the date reported precedes the date when the account was placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action. Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Duties of Financial Institutions When Reporting Negative Information Financial institutions that furnish information to nationwide consumer reporting agencies, as defined in Section 603 ( p ), must notify consumers in writing if they may furnish or have furnished negative information to a CRA. Section 623 ( a ) ( 7 ). The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has prescribed model disclosures, 12 CFR Part 1022, App. B.

Duties When Furnishing Medical Information A furnisher whose primary business is providing medical services, products, or devices ( and such furnisher 's agents or assignees ) is a medical information furnisher for the purposes of the FCRA and must notify all CRAs to which it reports of this fact. Section 623 ( a ) ( 9 ). This notice will enable CRAs to comply with their duties under Section 604 ( g ) when reporting medical information.

Duties when ID Theft Occurs All furnishers must have in place reasonable procedures to respond to notifications from CRAs that information furnished is the result of identity theft, and to prevent refurnishing the information in the future. A furnisher may not furnish information that a consumer has identified as resulting from identity theft unless the furnisher subsequently knows or is informed by the consumer that the information is correct. Section 623 ( a ) ( 6 ). If a furnisher learns that it has furnished inaccurate information due to identity theft, it must notify each consumer reporting agency of the correct information and must thereafter report only complete and accurate information. Section 623 ( a ) ( 2 ). When any furnisher of information is notified pursuant to the procedures set forth in Section 605B that a debt has resulted from identity theft, the furnisher may not sell, transfer, or place for collection the debt except in certain limited circumstances. Section 615 ( f ).

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website, consumerfinance.gov/learnmore, has more information about the FCRA.

Consumer complaint narrative:
1. Failure to Provide Conclusive Proof of Authorization The Bank claims that I authorized the Apple Card account opened on XX/XX/year>. This assertion is wholly unsubstantiated. To date, the Bank has failed to provide : Evidence of my explicit consent to open the account, including the specific device, IP address, and geolocation data tied to the application process ; Proof that any identity verification measures were employed during the account application process, as required under anti-fraud regulations and industry best practices. 
The mere existence of a transaction history and a generic cardholder agreement does not constitute evidence that I authorized this account. If the Bank is unable to demonstrate unequivocally that I opened and authorized the account, the account and any associated debts are invalid and must be removed immediately from all records. 

2. Flawed and Insufficient Investigation The Bank alleges that it conducted an investigation and determined no Bank error occurred. However, this investigation lacks transparency and appears cursory at best. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), the Bank is obligated to conduct a thorough investigation of any disputed information. Specifically, the Bank must : Verify the legitimacy of the account by examining the authorization process ; Consider the possibility of identity theft or fraud, given my explicit denial of authorization ; Provide clear and documented evidence supporting its findings. 
The Banks failure to meet these requirements renders its investigation legally inadequate. A generic statement of no Bank error is insufficient under the law and unacceptable in this case. 

3. Violation of Credit Reporting Obligations The Bank claims it is obligated to report accurate information to credit reporting agencies. While this is true, the obligation to report accurate information applies only to accounts that are legitimate. Reporting information on an account that was not authorized by me constitutes a blatant violation of FCRA 1681s-2 ( a ). The law explicitly prohibits the furnishing of inaccurate or incomplete information to credit reporting agencies. 

By continuing to report this account despite my explicit denial of authorization, the Bank is compounding its violation of federal law. The existence of this unauthorized account on my credit report has caused me significant harm, including : A decrease in my creditworthiness ; Financial damages related to higher interest rates and lost opportunities ; Emotional distress resulting from the Banks actions. 
4. Failure to Address or Prevent Fraud The Bank claims to have sent account statements, payment reminders, and other correspondence to the email address on file. However, as I have denied any authorization or involvement with this account, any such email address was likely associated with a fraudster. This raises serious questions about the Banks diligence in verifying the identity of applicants and monitoring for unauthorized account activity. 

Under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act ( GLBA ) and other relevant regulations, the Bank is required to take reasonable measures to protect consumers from fraud. The Banks reliance on email notifications and its failure to detect or address potential fraud represent a breach of its duty to safeguard my personal information and mitigate unauthorized activity. 

5. Insufficient Debt Validation The Bank claims to have validated the debt by providing transaction records and a copy of the Apple Card Customer Agreement. However, this is insufficient under 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ) of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ). Debt validation requires more than a generic agreement or a list of transactionsit requires proof that I : Authorized the account and incurred the alleged debt ; and Received the goods or services for which the debt was incurred. 
The documents provided by the Bank fail to meet this standard. Without proof of my consent, the Banks claims of debt validation are baseless. 

6. The Banks Inability to Contact Me The Bank asserts that it attempted to contact me but was unsuccessful. This claim is irrelevant and does not absolve the Bank of its responsibility to resolve this dispute properly. I have made multiple efforts to dispute this account, including through the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ). The Banks failure to contact me is not the result of my inaction, but rather its own inadequacy in handling this matter.

7. Demands for Immediate Action Based on the foregoing, I demand the following actions : Immediate Removal of the Account from All Credit Reports : The Bank must cease reporting this unauthorized account and ensure its deletion from all credit reporting agencies. Reporting an account that I did not authorize constitutes a willful violation of the FCRA.

Compensation for Damages : I reserve the right to seek compensation for actual damages, statutory damages, and punitive damages under FCRA 1681n for the harm caused by the Banks willful noncompliance.

Full Documentation of the Investigation : Provide all records, notes, and communications related to the Banks investigation of this dispute, including evidence relied upon to determine that no error occurred.

Failure to comply with these demands will leave me with no choice but to escalate this matter further, including filing a formal complaint with federal and state regulators and pursuing legal remedies. Please consider this letter a formal notice of my intent to take legal action if the matter is not resolved promptly. 

I expect a detailed response to this letter within 14 days.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I have a general purpose credit card with Home Depot. This credit card was used by an unknown individual to make a very large purchase ( > {$12000.00} ). The purchase was substantially all of the credit limit available on the card. The charge was made in store during XX/XX/year>. 

The charge was for the following items : XXXX XXXX gallon hot water tanks, XXXX XXXX flood light camera, XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXnd shower faucet, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX cordless tool set, XXXX bundles of red oak wood flooring, XXXX bundles of XXXX XXXX solid hard wood. 
These purchases appear to be from some sort of construction contractor and not typically something you'd expect to see on a personal credit card.

For a purchase this large, you would expect to require some sort of proof of identification and require a signature. 

I immediately disputed the charge through the Company 's online credit card platform. It was initially removed, pending investigation, however, months later it was placed back on the card. After calling multiple times to figure out what happened, the investigating team would not provide an adequate explanation as to why or how they determined the legitimacy of the charge.

I began the process of filing a policy report with the police department so that I had something on file. The police department informed me that they do not handle credit card theft/disputes/fraudulent activities and to follow the dispute process available through the Company website. 

I consistently made my claim that the charge was fraudulent and that I wanted to understand what steps were taken by the investigating team. I asked for details pertaining to who they spoke with, if they viewed or have copies of the in-store video footage, etc. I was never provided this detail, yet they concluded that the charge was legitimate. 

I continued to dispute the charge and had them re-open the investigation. Unfortunately, the same scenario played out where I was never contacted by anyone for further information. I only realized that the investigation had been closed when I saw the charge back to my account. Again, I called multiple times to get to the bottom of the investigation and conclusions reached but still got no where. 

Now the charge has been filed as delinquent by Home Depot and it appears on my credit report as a delinquent/missed payments.

It is not fair to a consumer who is not responsible for a significant charge to get no valid explanation for the conclusions reached, to have to constantly deal with the stress of a massive credit card bill that was not theirs, and to also have their credit report negatively affected.

I don't know what else to do about this fraudulent charge, how to get it off of my credit card/credit report, and how to repair my damaged credit report.

I immediately logged on to XXXX. Again, there were no orders matching this description or amount in my history. However, I clicked on the Customer Service link and THERE the order showed up. Again, not in my order history at all but only inside their Customer Service link. The system asked if I had questions about this order. I began a virtual chat with a representative who asked if I wanted to cancel the order. I stated that I did, but also expressed concern that it was a fake order. I asked if I needed to do anything else. They advised me that they cancelled the order and nothing else needed to be done. I was at work at the time, so I ended the chat intending to follow-up further after work. 
Very soon after my chat ended, however, I received additional shipment notifications of items both within that original order and additional items I had not yet seen. Panicked now, I called in to XXXX. I also logged on and saw in real time that items were even more items in my cart that I was not ordering. I spoke with a gentleman at length. He let me know that there were XXXX total orders totaling {$3500.00}. Each order was close to, but not above {$900.00}. He said that it appeared that they had added a stolen credit card and then later deleted this card in my account. He told me that it was clearly fraud. He suggested that I change my password on both XXXX and my email, add dual authentication and keep an eye on my credit card just in case. He said it was cancelled, but IF I did see charges come through to just dispute them. He assured me that it was clearly noted as fraud on XXXX end and they would not push back against any dispute. He stated that I would get an email with any instructions. I did receive an email with instructions only to do what he has suggested, and that I had already done. 
Over the next day or so after being out of the house, I returned home to find countless packages piled on my front stoop. I took pictures of the boxes. I called XXXX again. I asked them what to do with all of these packages that I did not order. I was told that, again, it was clearly marked as fraud and that I would receive an email once it had been investigated. I mentioned to the gentleman that I had no order so I could not start a return. I told him that the scam made absolutely no sense to me, as they delivered the packages to me. However, they did order a gift card that they appear to have sent to themselves, as part of this scam. I stacked the packages in my bedroom. The email that came once again advised me to change my password, add dual authentication, etc. which I had already done.

They said that I need to call the vendor, and that there is nothing else they can or will do. They did tell me that they could send me a copy of the statement that XXXX sent to them. I was told that they would escalate it internally and I would receive an email with the results. I asked if I could speak to the team it was being escalated to, and was told no. I asked if I could speak to a supervisor. The first gentleman told me that I could but placed me on hold for 45 minutes. Eventually he came back and suggested that I hang up and call right back in. He said he would note my account and I could ask that person to be transferred right away to their supervisor since his was not readily available. I did so, and the woman I spoke with the second time absolutely refused to transfer me to anyone else. Again, I was told that it was escalated, and would take 7-10 business days to receive a reply. I asked if the number for this team would be available on this reply, and she said no. I can not speak to anyone. I called in one more time and was told by the final person that again, it was clearly marked as fraud. How can they KNOW that it is fraud, admit that it is fraud to the point of not even including it in my order history, yet dispute that it is fraud with my credit card company? 
I would HAPPILY sign a release allowing a representative to read any call notes at XXXX and/or listen to any of my 10 or so recorded calls with them as I am 100 % confident that it will prove everything that I have disclosed in this letter. 
I beg you for help. Consumers are powerless against a corporation like this. Please do not allow them to simply steal from your constituents.

According to ( CFPB ) Consumer Finance Protection Bureau, 1026.56 Requirements for Over the Limit Transactions, Sub-section B ( Opt-In Requirement GENERAL ( 1 ) ; it states that a card issuer shall not assess a fee or charge on a consumers credit card account under the open-end ( not home-secured ) consumer credit plan for an over the limit transaction ( i.e. interest rates that exceed the credit limit on purpose with the sole intent to make a profit, cash advance fees that exceed the credit limit, return payment fees that exceed the credit limit, etc. ) unless the card issuer : ( i ) provides the consumer with an oral, written or electronic notice, segregated from all the other information, describing the consumers right to affirmatively consent, or opt in, to the card issuers payment of an over the limit transaction ; ( ii ) provides a reasonable opportunity for the consumer to affirmatively consent, or opt in, to the card issuers payment of over-the limit transactions, ( iii ) obtains the consumers affirmative consent, or opt-in, to the card issuers payment of such transactions, ( iv ) provides the consumer with confirmation of the consumers consent in writing or if the consumer agrees, electronically; and ( v ) provides the consumer notice in writing of the right to REVOKE that consent following the assessment of an over-the limit fee or charge. ( XXXX ) COMPLETION OF OVER THE LIMIT TRANSACTIONS WTIHOUT CONSUMER CONSENT. Notwithstanding the absence of a consumers affirmative consent under paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) ( iii ) of this section, a card issuer may pay any over-the-limit transaction on a consumers account provided that the card issuer does not impose a fee or charge on the account for paying that over-the-limit transaction. ( c ) Method of Election : a card issuer may permit a consumer to consent to the card issuers payment of any over the limit transaction in writing, orally, or electronically, at the card issuers option. The card issuer must also permit the consumer to revoke his or her consent using the same methods available to the consumer for providing consent. ( d ) Timing and Place of Notices : Initial Notice ; ( i ) General : The notice required by paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) ( i ) of this section shall be provided prior to the assessment of any over-the-limit fee or charge on a consumers consent. ( ii ) Oral or electronic consent : if a consumer consents to the card issuers payment of any over the limit transaction by oral or electronic means, the card issuer must provide the notice required by paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) ( i ) of this section immediately prior to obtaining this consent. ( 2 ) Confirmation of opt in : The notice required by paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) ( iv ) of this section may not be provided no later than the first periodic statement sent after the consumer has consented to the card issuers payment of over the limit transactions. ( 3 ) Notice of right revocation : The notice required by paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) ( v ) of this section shall be provided on the front of any page of each periodic statement that reflects the assessment of an over-the-limit fee or charge on a consumers account.
