Consumer complaint narrative:
Summary : I've been a Lowes/MVP customer for several years with thousands of dollars of purchases. This is a case of what I see as deceptive, breaching and burdensome practices relating to a promotional purchase for {$1000.00} pay-over-18 months - that was instead taken from my bank account in full at the next bill. In a subsequent chat ( below ), the Lowes servicer Synchrony claimed that their ability to manage automatic payments between regular and promotional purchases " is not yet available. '' XXXX XXXX, on the other hand, can allocate and has for years, and has a method by which the customer can even allocate payments themselves - I've done it for a {$13000.00} purchase. 

Lowes/Synchrony thinks it acceptable to agree to a pay-over-time contract with existing customers, then take the full amount of the customer 's money out of their bank, and then place the burden on the customer to call - but within 60 days of the " transaction date '' ( sic ) - and untangle a mess they didn't make. How many other unsuspecting customers have they done this to? 

Lowes/Synchrony excuses are not credible, and nowhere in their statement 's fine print or their topic-specific webpage " What is a Deferred Interest Promotion '' at https : //www.synchrony.com/consumer-resources/deferred-interest - do they say they aren't able to allocate promotional payments. They don't warn the customer that the entire promotional balance could be immediately deducted, but suggest you call ( within 60 days of the transaction ) into an overseas call center and " learn what options are available, '' which I did, below. 

On XX/XX/XXXX during a 40 minute call, I endured how this scheme created a lucrative opportunity for Lowes/Synchrony to hurriedly change the customer 's automatic payment amounts from the interest-saving " total statement balance '' to " total minimum payment '' - which I let them do to see if they would actually do this- which then brings an interest rate of an astonishing 32 % to bear - 37 %! if late - a usurious detail they must be carefully trained not to mention. 

The Bureau needs to protect consumers from this behavior and admonish and instruct Lowes/Synchrony to implement a functioning payment allocation system that works at the time of purchase when the promotional contract is made - and not instead put the burden on the customer to call in later to disentangle a hidden mess they didn't make. Lowes/Synchrony breached this pay over time promotional offer by debiting the full {$1000.00} amount immediately, causing me harm by reducing my bank account unexpectedly and imperiling other payment obligations I have. 

Companies like Lowes/Synchrony just don't seem to understand that once they break the trust like this with a customer, they will always be remembered as an untrustworthy partner the moment you think of shopping there. 

Resolution : ( below on CFPB form ) All the Details : For years, I've had my Lowes autopay set to pay the " total statement balance '' in full each month to avoid carrying interest charges. On XX/XX/XXXX I purchased a tow behind trailer for {$1000.00}. I elected to take up their offer of 18 month " reg deferred interest with pay '' same-as-cash minimum payment option that they heavily promote everywhere in the store and on their statements, rather than pay-in-full and enjoy an also heavily promoted pay now discount of 5 %, in this case {$51.00}. 

Four months of statements needed deciphering. The next paperless statement with a payment due date of XX/XX/XXXX ( there are no " statement dates '' ), I see both the " promotion expiration notification '' in red ink and then the usual " promotional purchase summary '' box, each showing an expiration in 18 months on XX/XX/XXXX. Easily overlooked, especially with autopay and on paperless statements that require a login and several clicks to obtain the bill, is the autopay message in a different XXXX showing a {$1000.00} payment scheduled. Instead, you see it shows a minimum payment due of {$30.00}. 

On the next statement dated XX/XX/XXXX, the ENTIRE {$1000.00} " promotional '' balance was taken from my bank, completely disregarding the promotional agreement terms. 

Meaning, instead of waiting the 18 months that we clearly agreed to ( with minimum payments ), they snatched the entire {$1000.00} all at once, without a care what this large debit could do to the customer 's cash flow and other bills. And then, they put the burden on the customer to call up and disentangle a mess they didn't create, dealing with trained and scripted representatives and long hold times, hoping - as is widely known in the industry - that the customer will hang up. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I called their XXXX number and was sent to an overseas non-native-english language speaking call center for a 40 minute call with a 15 minute hold. I also initiated a chat window. 

In the chat, I say Customer : " my 18 month promotional balance was entirely deducted from my bank account. doesn't your autopay distinguish promo balances from new purchases? '' and they reply : L/S : " autopay only has XXXX options to choose from with regards to payment amount. In addition, autopay doesn't distinguish what the promotional balance is. '' and then : L/S : " I'm sorry if the feature is not available yet with our autopay. '' I then say that I want that {$1000.00} that was deducted from my bank account returned to me. Then, what seems to be a supervisor suddenly appears and says : L/S : " Oops! My wires got crossed for a second. I may have missed something. Can you please try again? '' and then says " How much is the amount of the refund you are requesting from the {$1000.00}? '' Simultaneously, on the phone, the representative then hurried me through the needless process of " enrolling me in autopay '' ( I was already enrolled for years ), not disclosing that they signed me up with the " total minimum payment '' option instead of " total statement balance, '' which then subjects my balances to 32 % APR. I listened for this very carefully. Then, with hurried assurances that they'll send a refund check if approved, they say they're not able to provide a case number " until the refund gets approved. '' A refund check for {$1100.00} arrived at my home around XX/XX/XXXX. 

In the next statement for XX/XX/XXXX, the " promotional purchase summary '' box is gone, no mention anywhere of the pay over time agreement we contracted to. Instead, Lowes/Synchrony debited the {$1100.00} as a " refund check '', and added it as a regular interest-bearing purchase, pushing my balance due up by almost {$1200.00}. All subject to 32 % interest. I waited to see what they would do next, to collect documentation. 

A month later on the next statement for XX/XX/XXXX, the " promotional purchase summary '' box is suddenly back, there's now a credit for {$1000.00} labelled " promotion correction, '' which they restored as a pay over time purchase, and then added a {$2.00} cash grab termed " minimum interest charge. '' Conclusion : So, almost 5 months after making a substantial purchase with the clear understanding that I could pay the cost over time, then suddenly being stripped of my funds right from my bank, and then having to endure a slippery call center call experience, followed by more months of having to decipher confusing statements, we're back to where we started - except I'm out several hours and more of figuring this out and worrying what Lowes/Synchrony will do next.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/2024, my credit card was charged by XXXX XXXX in the amount of {$980.00}. Subsequently, I noticed a billing error in the amount of {$240.00} and have made several attempts to contact the merchant and resolve this billing error. Unfortunately the merchant never responded to my multiple communications. 

On XX/XX/2024, I initiated a credit card billing dispute with Barclays. The dispute case ID is XXXX. 

On XX/XX/2024, Barclays sent me a copy of merchant response to my billing dispute. The merchant response itemized billing items, including the item that was billed in error. I provided additional supporting documentation to Barclays to explain the billing error. 

On XX/XX/2024 and XX/XX/2024, I received additional communications from Barclays notifying the case is closed without resolving the billing error. No further documentary evidence was provided by Barclays to explain its decision. 

In accordance to the section 1666 ( a ) ( B ) ( ii ) of the Fair Credit Billing Act, the creditor shall send a written explanation or clarification to the obligor, after having conducted an investigation, setting forth to the extent applicable the reasons why the creditor believes the account of the obligor was correctly shown in the statement and, upon request of the obligor, provide copies of documentary evidence of the obligor 's indebtedness. In the case of a billing error where the obligor alleges that the creditor 's billing statement reflects goods not delivered to the obligor or his designee in accordance with the agreement made at the time of the transaction, a creditor may not construe such amount to be correctly shown unless he determines that such goods were actually delivered, mailed, or otherwise sent to the obligor and provides the obligor with a statement of such determination.

By closing this billing dispute without providing documentary evidence to support its decision, Barclays has violated the Fair Credit Billing Act.

THE TRANSACTION In a credit card securitization transaction only the receivables are sold, not the accounts that generate the receivables. The financial institution retains legal ownership of the credit card accounts and can continue to change the terms on the accounts. Accounts corresponding to securitized loans are typically referred to as the designated accounts ( or sometimes trust accounts ). The initial outstanding balances on the designated accounts are sold to the trust as are the rights to any new charges on the designated accounts. Subsequently, as cardholder purchase activity generates more receivables on the designated accounts, these new receivables are purchased by the trust from the originating institution/seller/transferor. Consumer complaint narrative:
My intention was to maintain an active account and settle my balance under the terms of a 12-month payment arrangement plan which I was informed of during a call on XX/XX/XXXX. However, due to a failure in communication and guidance from their representatives during this call and during the scheduled follow-up call on XX/XX/XXXX, my account was closed, despite my best efforts to comply with the instructions provided. 

This situation arose from several critical errors, which I have outlined in the chronological timeline below. On XX/XX/XXXX, I complied with a letter I received on XX/XX/XXXX to call Apple Card Customer Support regarding my past due amount. At this time, the representative enrolled me in a one-month deferral with clear instructions to call back and enroll in a payment plan on XX/XX/XXXX, following the deferral. My intentions were to keep the account in good standing, which would occur after 12 lowered monthly payments, at 0 % APR. At no point was I informed during this phone call that the collections department, not customer service ( whom I had called ), was handling the 1 month deferral and was providing the financial product information ( the 12 month arrangement ) and instructions on when to call back and enroll in the payment arrangement. I was advised to call back on XX/XX/XXXX, after taking full advantage of the deferral time period, as a payment needed to be made on the same date of enrollment into the 12 month payment arrangement. At this time, I was neither informed I needed to speak with this specific department, meaning the Collections Department, or made aware of their limited operating hours until XXXX XXXX. Apple Customer service makes it very clear, via the XXXX XXXX, that Customer Service is available XXXX. I would eventually find out, during the Tier 2 Manager investigation, that due to the status of my account, and making the XX/XX/XXXX call during normal operating hours, my call was automatically routed through the phone system from the general Customer Service extension I called in from and directed to Collections Department whom had handled my XX/XX/XXXX call. This error in omission is the reason I could not complete the enrollment in the 12 month payment arrangement when I called XX/XX/XXXX. 

As planned, I called back Customer Service on the night of XX/XX/XXXX. I was informed by the representative that the specific department ( unnamed ) I needed to speak to had closed 1 hour prior to my calling. I expressed confusion and concern because I was told that this was the date that I needed to enroll in the payment arrangement plan and was worried my account would close that day if not done. The representative essentially told me not to worry and call back during their normal operating hours, before XXXX. With this new information, I was still under the assumption that Customer Service had provided the original deferral on XX/XX/XXXX and perhaps, now, payment arrangements were handled by this unnamed other department. The call was brief. I was not provided with any further information on my account and there was no explicit communication of when I needed to take action on the payment and would do so when convenient. 

Following the investigation into the closure, I found that this representative took no action on my account to notify the correct team that I called and made an attempt to enroll into the payment program. There were in fact, no notes from this call on my account. It was not until the transcript of the call was reviewed that the contents on the conversation, and the intentions to enroll, were made clear to the investigating team. During my XX/XX/XXXX call, the representative ( whom I still considered Customer Service ) performed a thorough review of my account and recent communications with Apple Card before providing me with payment options. I assumed the XX/XX/XXXX representative had done this review after the verification process when I called in. A review should have provided me with two ( 2 ) critical pieces of information - ( 1 ) That I received an email on XX/XX/XXXX stating to call Apple Card Support by XX/XX/XXXX ; and ( 2 ) That a payment had to be made by XX/XX/XXXX to avoid closure. I explained to the investigating Manager that had I known this, I would have made a payment on that date rather than delaying my first payment to coincide with the enrollment in the 12mo payment arraignment. I never read the email because I had already created a plan with a representative on XX/XX/XXXX and the call on XX/XX/XXXX was within the timeframe given on the XX/XX/XXXX email anyway- I would still have called in the same number. If a customer calls Apple Card Support a review should be done and any urgent actions needed to be taken on the account should have been communicated. My call actually met the requirement of the letter to contact Apple Card Support by XX/XX/XXXX. The investigating Manager stated that Customer Service representatives are not trained to perform an account review. How am I to know what level of training to expect from a representative when I called in? My only expectation is consistency. I called the same Customer Support number I had on XX/XX/XXXX and expected the same level of care and diligence. I can only now assume that had I called before XXXX XXXX, I would have likely been automatically routed to the Collections Department for a proper account review, where I would have also been able to complete the enrollment in the payment arrangement as planned. I believe it was this lack of training and diligence in reviewing my account during the XX/XX/XXXX call that led to the erroneous closure of my account. Even though I was not enrolled in a payment plan yet, I felt this call at least satisfied the requirement of contacting Apple by this date and if there was any change in the status of my account after this communication, such as its impending closure, I would be notified by Apple Card at such time- I was not and, unknown to me, the account went into closure on XX/XX/XXXX. 

I followed up on XX/XX/XXXX call one week later on XX/XX/XXXX. I spoke with a XXXX Department agent, XXXX, who confirmed that my account was closed. After I discussed the previous conversations, he stated that closure was likely an error and reassured me that because I was promised a payment arrangement ( which could not be performed by the agent I spoke with during the XX/XX/XXXX call, on the date I was instructed to call back on ) Apple Card would need to honor that arrangement and my account would be reopened. I was told I would receive a call back within 10 days once the process was complete, which also included a review of the account to verify the events. During a subsequent follow-up on XX/XX/XXXX, a Manager ( unnamed ) called back and insisted the closure was not an error. I argued all the points Ive previously made in this letter but she was still insistent it was not an error. We were at an impasse, I wanted answers and an escalation. She roadblocked me saying she was the final authority on determining whether it was an error or not. She refused an escalation and I questioned what authority she had in determining what an Error qualified as because there were several opportunities for Apple Card to prevent the closure. She quickly became offensive, telling me the closure was all my fault and I shouldve just paid the bill on time. It was crass and unprofessional and her when I requested her identification, she hung up on me! 

I immediately called back and spoke with another XXXX Department agent, XXXX, and filed a complaint. When I calmed down, I said I do not want to wait another 10 days for an additional review and I wanted to speak with his supervisor so I can come to some sort of resolution that day. I was connected to his supervisor, XXXX, who stated she was the same level of authority as the Manager who hung up on me - a Tier 2 supervisor. We had the same conversation and I was met with the same stonewalling as the previous conversation. While she admitted it was improper, all I heard were excuses regarding the phone routing system, the lack of training of the Customer Service reps and the omissions of where and to whom I needed to make the payment arrangement with and by what time. This is all after the fact. These are clearly errors but she would not acknowledge it as such. It felt as if she was trained not to acknowledge wrong doing because such an admission would require actual escalation and the reopening of a closed account. We concluded the conversation with XXXX escalating the issue for a second review which should could not guarantee would escalate to Tier 3, but at a minimum it would be reviewed by a Tier 2 Manager. At the date I am writing this letter, it was been 37 days since that phone call and I have yet to receive any further communication. 

The following timeline illustrates the sequence of events leading to this complaint : Timeline of Events 1. XX/XX/XXXX : Received notice stating that my account was past due and I had to call before XX/XX/XXXX to prevent permanent closure. 
2. XX/XX/XXXX : I called customer service and was enrolled in a one-month deferral, with instructions to call back on XX/XX/XXXX to enroll in a 12-month payment arrangement with a lowered monthly payment and 0 % APR. 
3. XX/XX/XXXX : Called back to enroll in the 12-month plan, but I was told that the department responsible had just closed an hour earlier. No specific department was mentioned during this call. Advised to call back. 
4. XX/XX/XXXX : Called customer service and was informed that my account had been closed since XX/XX/XXXX. Spoke with XXXX, who confirmed the closure and initiated the review process to reopened the account after a supervisor investigation. 
5. XX/XX/XXXX : Spoke with a customer service manager who denied that the closure was an error. After a verbal altercation, I asked for her identification and she hung up. 
6. XX/XX/XXXX : Spoke with XXXX and XXXX. XXXX confirmed the miscommunications but would not admit fault. She escalated the issue for an additional review. 
7. Present : No further communication has been received regarding the resolution, and the account remains closed.

I called Citibank on XX/XX/XXXX and confirmed that, because the {$8.00} was not collected, Citibank decided to slap a {$30.00} fine on my account for the 3-day payment delay, regardless of the fact that my bank autopay disruption was neither caused by me, nor of my knowledge.

I immediately paid off the {$8.00} outstanding balance, requested Citibank to waive the {$30.00} returned check fees, and closed my credit card account in the same call. I thought me being such a loyal and well-behaving customer for over 8 years, this humble request would definitely be honored. 
Was I wrong! 
On XX/XX/XXXX, Citibank issued me another email saying my payment was past due. By then I have already traveled overseas to visit my family in XXXX. Very surprised I went back to check my closed credit card account, and found out not only did Citibank refuse to waive the {$30.00} returned check fees, but also imposed another {$30.00} late fees and {$0.00} interest charge onto my account, making the outstanding balance to more than doubled, rapidly growing from {$30.00} to {$60.00}!

She said she was able to waive the newer {$30.00} late fees right away for me. As for the {$30.00} returned check fees and the {$0.00} interest charges she would need to write a report and get her supervisors approval. She said that she was hopeful such requests would be honored and she would write me an email to sum up all the issues.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing a formal complaint against Chase Bank concerning the denial of my application for a Chase Edge credit card on XX/XX/year>. I believe that this denial involved violations of federal consumer protection laws, specifically under 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( Equal Credit Opportunity Act ) and 12 CFR 1002 ( Regulation B ). 

Chase Bank provided the following reasons for the denial : History of poor credit performance Too few accounts with recent payment information Revolving accounts not paid as agreed Current or past bankruptcy, charge-offs, public records, judgments, tax liens, or collections I contend that these reasons are unlawful grounds for denying credit under 15 U.S.C. 1691 and 12 CFR 1002, which prohibit adverse action based on credit score, credit history, or income without a legitimate, legally justified basis. 

Detailed Explanation : 1. Unlawful Denial Based on Credit Score, Credit History, or Income : Under 15 U.S.C. 1691 and 12 CFR 1002, it is illegal to deny credit based on credit score, credit history, or income unless there is a legally justified basis directly tied to creditworthiness. The reasons provided for my denial suggest these prohibited factors were used, which would constitute a violation of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. 
2. Adverse Actions in Consumer Credit Transactions : Any adverse action in a consumer credit transaction, as communicated by Chase Bank, should comply with all applicable laws. Denial based solely on credit score, credit history, or income without a clear, legitimate, and lawful justification is not permissible under federal regulations.
